text.p: The mark received a fillip in late Europe when Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said its fall against the dollar could not continue at its recent pace.

But traders said dealings had been choppy as the market puzzled over Welteke's comments that the U.S. unit's strength had boosted German exports and he saw no danger of inflation being imported into Germany.

"One minute he's saying the mark's slide cannot continue... then he's saying they're pretty happy with the way things have been going with the dollar," said Martin Ely, senior manager head of proprietary trading at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
"What's surprising is not what he said but that he took so long to say it," said Nick Parsons, forex strategist at Banque Paribas in London.
"The danger is that the longer they don't say anything, the more difficult it will ultimately be to exercise their traditional control over the market," he added.
Although the session saw dollar/mark soar to a fresh 31-month high as the U.S. currency roared ahead across the board, the mark avoided suffering on the crosses.
Traders said dollar buying against European currencies had helped depress them versus the mark.
The market is also awaiting the release of German M3 money supply data for December, forecast on average to show growth slowing to 7.5 percent from 8.0 in November.

The Italian lira was quoted at 972.35/85 marks at 1537 GMT, down from late Tuesday's European level of 970.90/1.20. The Bank of Italy's interest rate cuts yesterday took some steam out of the lira but had not weakened it unduly, analysts said.

Nordic currencies, which have rallied dramatically recently, gave back small portions of their gains. The markka fell to 2.9410/30 per mark from late yesterday's 2.9320, while the Norwegian crown stood at 3.9820/70 versus 3.9710.
The Bundesbank holds its regular council meeting tomorrow, but most economists polled by Reuters expect no change in interest rates to emerge.
